questions.stem: James March's classical distinction in organisational learning is between:
questions.explanation: March (1991) framed organisational learning as a tension between exploitation (refining what you already do) and exploration (searching for new possibilities).

questions.stem: Tushman & O'Reilly's 'ambidextrous organisation' resolves the exploration-exploitation tension by:
choices: Choosing one mode and ignoring the other.
Structurally separating exploitation and exploration units, with senior leadership integrating them.
questions.explanation: Ambidextrous orgs run both modes in parallel with distinct structures, metrics, and culture. Senior leadership protects exploration from being killed by the exploitation immune system.

questions.stem: The McKinsey Three Horizons framework typically allocates investment approximately:
questions.explanation: The classical 70/20/10 split: 70% to defending the core, 20% to building emerging businesses, 10% to long-term options.

questions.stem: The Stage-Gate process is most associated with:
questions.explanation: Robert Cooper developed the Stage-Gate methodology for new product development from the 1980s onward.

questions.stem: At each gate in Cooper's Stage-Gate process, the decision is typically:
questions.explanation: Each gate is a structured Go / Kill / Hold / Recycle decision against explicit criteria by a cross-functional committee — early kills reduce waste.

questions.stem: The innovation portfolio matrix typically uses which two axes?
questions.explanation: The standard innovation portfolio matrix maps existing/new market against existing/new technology, producing four quadrants from incremental to breakthrough.

questions.stem: Which quadrant of the innovation portfolio matrix represents the HIGHEST risk and HIGHEST potential?
questions.explanation: New-market + new-technology is breakthrough territory: highest uncertainty, highest reward. Most firms keep limited exposure here as part of a balanced portfolio.

questions.stem: Which Miles & Snow strategic archetype matches a firm that LEADS with new products and markets (e.g. Tesla, early Apple)?
questions.explanation: Prospectors lead with innovation and explore aggressively. High risk, high upside. Tesla and early Apple are textbook examples.

questions.stem: A common CRITICISM of the classical Stage-Gate process is that:
choices: It allows too much spending on weak projects.
It is too rigid for radical innovation; the linear stages and detailed business cases stifle iteration.
It eliminates the need for product managers.
questions.explanation: Stage-Gate works well for incremental/sustaining innovation but is too slow and structured for radical or disruptive innovation. Hence agile stage-gate hybrids.

questions.stem: March argued that organisations naturally OVER-INVEST in exploitation because:
choices: Exploration is more expensive in absolute terms.
Exploitation has clearer metrics and faster, more predictable payoffs that internal reward systems favour.
Exploration is illegal in some jurisdictions.
questions.explanation: Performance-management systems reward measurable near-term outcomes. Exploration's diffuse and delayed payoffs lose every budget cycle without senior protection.

questions.stem: Cisco's historical 'spin-in' model and IBM's Emerging Business Opportunities programme are examples of:
questions.explanation: Both create structurally separated vehicles for exploration with senior oversight bridging back to the core business. Textbook ambidexterity.

questions.stem: An 'agile stage-gate' hybrid:
choices: Integrates iterative agile / lean-startup loops within each stage, while keeping gates for major capital decisions.
questions.explanation: Agile stage-gate keeps the discipline of major capital gates while allowing each stage to run iterative loops — best of both worlds for many corporates.

questions.stem: Google's historical '20% time' is best understood as:
choices: A structural mechanism for bottom-up exploration alongside the exploitation-heavy core (i.e. ambidexterity at the individual level).
questions.explanation: 20% time gave engineers structural permission to explore. Gmail and AdSense both originated this way. A bottom-up ambidexterity mechanism.

questions.stem: Which is the BIGGEST risk Tushman highlights when running exploration inside an exploitation-heavy firm WITHOUT structural separation?
choices: The exploitation 'immune system' (processes, metrics, salesforce, culture) kills the exploration unit before it matures.
questions.explanation: Without protected structure, exploration is judged by exploitation metrics (margin, predictability) it cannot satisfy. Senior leadership must shield it.

questions.stem: Which is a typical Horizon 3 investment for a tech firm?
choices: Cost reduction on the flagship product.
A speculative far-out bet such as quantum computing, drug discovery, or fusion energy.
A line extension into a neighbouring market.
questions.explanation: Horizon 3 = create viable options for the long term. Speculative deep tech is the canonical placement. Cost reduction and line extension are Horizon 1.

questions.stem: Approximately how many raw ideas become a single commercial success in classical innovation funnel statistics?
questions.explanation: The often-cited ratio: ~3000 ideas → ~4 launches → ~1 success. Whether your numbers vary, the order of magnitude is the lesson.

questions.stem: An incumbent company with 90% of revenue in a slow-growing product is best diagnosed as:
choices: Exploitation-heavy, requiring renewed investment in exploration
questions.explanation: Concentration in a slow-growing core indicates exploitation dominance. March's recommendation: rebalance toward exploration before disruption arrives.

questions.stem: A firm pursuing a 'fast follower' strategy that copies proven innovations from leaders while defending its core is best classified as a Miles & Snow:
questions.explanation: Analyzers hybridise: defend the core while copying proven innovations. Microsoft for much of the 2000s, Samsung in many product categories.

questions.stem: Which Miles & Snow archetype typically performs WORST?
questions.explanation: Reactors have no clear strategy and only respond to events. Empirically the worst-performing archetype across Miles & Snow's studies.

questions.stem: The 3M innovation pipeline famously sets which target?
choices: 100% of products less than 1 year old.
30% of revenue from products less than four years old.
10% R&D as a fraction of revenue.
questions.explanation: 3M's '30% from products under 4 years old' target forces continual exploration into the operating rhythm of the firm.

questions.stem: Crossing the chasm (Moore) is relevant to commercialisation strategy because:
choices: Innovations naturally transition from early adopters to mainstream without intervention.
Many promising innovations die in the gap between visionary early adopters and pragmatist early majority unless the firm shifts to a complete whole-product offering.
Chasms apply only to consumer markets.
questions.explanation: The chasm requires a transition from features-pitch to a complete solution (services, training, support, ecosystem). Many startups fail to make this transition.

questions.stem: Google's Loon balloon project (since shut down) was best classified as which horizon?
questions.explanation: Loon was a speculative long-term bet on connectivity — Horizon 3. Many Horizon 3 bets fail; that is the point of having a portfolio.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST reason to keep an exploration unit's METRICS distinct from the core business?
choices: Core metrics (margin, EBITDA, predictability) penalise the long, uncertain payoff of exploration; exploration needs validated-learning metrics (cohort retention, learning velocity).
questions.explanation: Wrong metrics will kill exploration on every reporting cycle. Distinct metrics align measurement with the work — Ries-style innovation accounting in the exploration unit.

questions.stem: A firm asks: 'Should we invest in this new technology even though it has lower margins than our core?' The strongest framework to apply is:
choices: Christensen's disruption + Tushman's ambidexterity — the lower-margin entrant may be a disruptor, and the response is a structurally separate explorer unit.
questions.explanation: The combination is exam-favoured: Christensen explains the threat (low margins = disruption signature); Tushman explains the organisational response (autonomous explorer unit).

questions.stem: An innovation portfolio that is HEAVILY skewed to incremental (existing market + existing tech) is:
choices: Short-term efficient but long-term vulnerable to disruption; needs rebalancing toward Horizon 2/3.
questions.explanation: Pure incremental innovation is the classical innovator's-dilemma posture: maximises near-term margin, leaves no defence against disruption. Portfolio rebalancing is the response.
